clinicalPearls: Presents in early infancy with faltering growth, frontal bossing and macrocephaly.
Obliteration of the marrow cavity causes anaemia, thrombocytopenic bleeding and susceptibility to infection.
Encroachment on skull foramina compresses cranial nerves, causing optic atrophy and blindness, deafness and facial palsy.
Bones are dense on radiographs yet mechanically brittle, so pathological fractures are common.
Impaired resorption limits calcium mobilisation, producing hypocalcaemia with secondary hyperparathyroidism that may cause tetany or seizures.
Genotype guides therapy: haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can cure osteoclast-intrinsic, osteoclast-rich disease but does not correct RANKL-dependent (osteoclast-poor) forms.
CLCN7- and OSTM1-related subtypes may show progressive neurodegeneration that transplantation does not prevent.
reference.pathophysiology: Autosomal recessive osteopetrosis results from failure of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, so that primary and woven bone are never remodelled into normal lamellar bone and the marrow cavity is progressively obliterated. The commonest cause is loss of function of TCIRG1, encoding the a3 subunit of the osteoclast vacuolar proton pump, which prevents acidification of the resorption lacuna; other genes include CLCN7 and its beta-subunit OSTM1, SNX10, and the RANK and RANKL signalling pair (TNFRSF11A and TNFSF11). In osteoclast-rich forms (for example TCIRG1, CLCN7, SNX10) osteoclasts are present but cannot resorb bone, whereas osteoclast-poor disease reflects failure of osteoclast generation, either from absent stromal RANKL or defective RANK on precursors. Dense but architecturally disordered bone is brittle and fracture-prone, encroaches on cranial foramina to compress the optic, facial and auditory nerves, and crowds out marrow to produce anaemia, thrombocytopenia and extramedullary haematopoiesis with hepatosplenomegaly. Deficient resorption also limits calcium mobilisation, causing hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism, and CLCN7- or OSTM1-related disease may additionally cause a primary neurodegeneration.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal dominant (adult) osteopetrosis and intermediate autosomal recessive forms
Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency (osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis and cerebral calcification)
Congenital leukaemia or other marrow infiltration causing pancytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly
Congenital (TORCH) infection with hepatosplenomegaly and metaphyseal changes
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey showing diffuse osteosclerosis, bone-in-bone appearance, rugger-jersey spine and loss of corticomedullary differentiation
Full blood count and blood film (anaemia, thrombocytopenia, leucoerythroblastic changes)
Serum calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D
Molecular genetic testing (TCIRG1, CLCN7, OSTM1, SNX10, TNFSF11, TNFRSF11A)
Cranial CT or MRI for foraminal stenosis, and brain MRI where neurodegeneration is suspected
Bone biopsy to characterise osteoclast number and morphology (osteoclast-rich versus osteoclast-poor)
redFlags: Progressive visual deterioration or optic atrophy
Severe pancytopenia with bleeding or sepsis
reference.prognosis: Without treatment the malignant infantile form is usually fatal in early childhood from marrow failure, haemorrhage or infection. Timely haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be curative in suitable osteoclast-rich subtypes, although established neurodegeneration and osteoclast-poor disease respond poorly.
pitfalls: Attributing the leucoerythroblastic pancytopenia to leukaemia and overlooking the diagnostic dense bones
Assuming all subtypes respond to transplantation, when osteoclast-poor (RANKL-dependent) disease does not
Reassuring families about fracture risk because the bones look dense, when they are actually brittle
Failing to institute cranial nerve surveillance, allowing preventable blindness or deafness
